A trimmed mean is a robust baseline strategy designed to handle this instability by ignoring the most extreme forecasts.
Test simple mean of top 5 performers to leverage diversity and mitigate ranking instability.

The ranking instability (tau=0.119) and high correlation suggest that simple pooling of top models works well by averaging out noise, but expanding to the full pool might introduce beneficial diversity from lower-ranked but uncorrelated models. I will test a weighted combination over the full pool using inverse error weights to leverage the best performers while allowing others to contribute proportionally.

The series has a strong trend (0.76) and unstable model rankings across windows (tau=0.119), suggesting that simple mean/median on a fixed pool might be suboptimal if we can exploit the recent window's dynamics where ARIMA was best. Since `pool4` (top 5 by overall RMSE) worked well with a simple mean, I will test a weighted combination of this same pool using inverse error weights to see if giving more power to the currently lower-error models (ETS, ARIMA) improves over the equal-weighted baseline.

The series has a strong trend (trend_strength=0.7635) and unstable ranking (ranking_tau=0.119). Current best uses inverse error weights on top 5 models. I want to test if softmax_neg_error weights, which dampen the influence of the absolute best model and give more weight to others, can better handle the instability by leveraging diversity within the top cluster.

The current leader (a4) uses a weighted combination on a top-5 pool with inverse error weights, scoring 0.9321. The ranking stability is very low (tau=0.119), suggesting that simple weighting by recent error might be unstable or that the "best" models are too correlated. A robust strategy like DBA (Discriminative Bias Adjustment) or a broad median/trimmed mean over a larger, more diverse pool might better handle the instability and capture the strong trend component without overfitting to specific window errors. I will test a DBA approach on the full pool to see if it can find a better bias correction than the current weighted ensemble.

The current leader (a4) uses a weighted combination of pool4. A different kind of strategy is needed to check if robust aggregation on the full or larger pool handles the unstable ranking better than the specific weighting of a4. I will test a simple median on pool5 (the k=7 top models), which provides robustness against outliers and model instability while leveraging more diversity than pool4.

The series has a strong trend (0.76) and unstable model rankings across windows (tau=0.12). Previous weighted strategies on pool4 were top contenders, but the leader diagnostics indicate the gap is indistinguishable from simple mean or other robust methods. To test a different kind of strategy that might better handle the non-stationary trend component without over-weighting potentially noisy recent errors, I will use `weights_error_trend` which adapts weights based on whether models are improving or degrading, applied to the full pool to maximize diversity and mitigate the risk of excluding a model that might suddenly excel due to trend shifts.

The series has a strong trend (0.76) and unstable model rankings across windows, suggesting that simple pooling of diverse models might be robust. Current leaders use small pools (top 5). I will test a broader mean combination of the top 19 models to see if leveraging the full ensemble's diversity mitigates the ranking instability better than the focused top-5 weighted approaches.

The current leader (a4) uses a weighted combination on a small top-5 pool with inverse error weights, but the margin to the runner-up is negligible and the ranking stability is low (tau=0.119). This suggests that rigid weight estimation may be overfitting noise. I will test a robust trimmed mean on the same top-5 pool to mitigate the impact of any potential outliers or mis-weighted models in this small subset, leveraging the series' strong trend but unstable ranking characteristics.

The current leader (a4) uses a weighted combination on pool4 (ETS, ARIMA, DWT_catboost, FT_catboost, ONLY_DWT_catboost). Since the ranking is unstable and the gap to the next best is negligible, I want to test if including the stable but slightly less accurate NaiveSeasonal (which won window 1) in a simple mean combination improves robustness against the strong trend. This tests the "robust" hint by broadening the pool to include different structural approaches while keeping it small.
Test robustness against ranking instability by trimming outliers from the top-performing pool6.

decision.justification: Selected 'mean on pool6' (an agent proposal) as the best of 12 backtested attempts, score 0.9027. Series context: trend strength 0.7635 and seasonal strength 0.3287; model ranking is unstable across windows (Kendall tau 0.119); 3 of 19 models carry independent error; relative error spread across the pool is 0.375.
